jelacic: Zagreb's main square, with the equestrian statue of Josip Jelačić, where the Upper Town and Lower Town meet. From here you walk through Donji Grad (the Lower Town) to Zrinjevac, the park with the bandstand, among 19th-century buildings.
dolac: Zagreb's most famous open-air market, behind the main square, with its red umbrellas. Fruit, vegetables, cheese, embroidery and flowers up top; meat and fish in the covered market below.
cathedral: The Cathedral of the Assumption, with two neo-Gothic spires over a hundred metres high, is Croatia's largest religious building. Around it is Kaptol, the old clergy quarter, with its palaces and squares.
tkalcic: The pedestrian lane lined with cafés and restaurants, running along the now-covered Medveščak stream between Kaptol and the Upper Town. It's Zagreb's aperitif street, with low, colourful houses.
stone: Stone Gate and St Mark's Church

In the Upper Town, the Stone Gate is the only surviving medieval gate of the walls: under the arch is a chapel with a Madonna believed to be miraculous. A little further on, St Mark's Church has a roof of coloured tiles with the coats of arms of Croatia and Zagreb, the city's most photographed sight.
broken: A small, original and very popular museum, born in Zagreb: it displays objects left by people all over the world after a love affair ended, each with its story written in English and Croatian. Read and wander slowly: the stories will make you laugh and cry.
lotr: Lotrščak Tower, funicular and Strossmayer Promenade

A 13th-century tower with a narrow staircase to the top floor and a 360-degree view over the rooftops. Every day at noon a cannon is fired from the tower. Next to it is the funicular, one of the shortest in the world, and the Strossmayer Promenade, a viewpoint with trees and benches.
gric: A tunnel under the Upper Town, built during the Second World War as an air-raid shelter: today it's a pedestrian passage linking Mesnička and Radićeva streets and hosting small exhibitions. A cool break in summer and shelter from the rain.
mirogoj: Considered one of Europe's most beautiful cemeteries, a large park with neo-Renaissance arcades and domes by Hermann Bollé, and the graves of figures from Croatian history. Rather than a sad place, it's a peaceful one to walk among trees and sculptures, in deep silence.
